Description: Malaria is a life-threatening but preventable and curable infectious disease. It is caused by Plasmodium parasites and is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. The greatest burden of malaria occurs in sub-Saharan Africa, including Ethiopi
Cause: Malaria is caused by five species of Plasmodium that infect humans. The two most important species are:               >  Plasmodium falciparum       >  Plasmodium vivax                 In Ethiopia, both species occur, but P. falciparum is responsible for many severe case
Risk_factors: People at higher risk of severe malaria include: > Children under 5 years                                    > Pregnant women         > People living with HIV/AIDS                              > Travelers without immunity                            > People living in malaria-endemic areas
Severity: Emergency level = High                  Reason: Malaria can rapidly become severe and life-threatening if not diagnosed and treated promptly.

Description: Tuberculosis (TB) is a preventable and curable infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It most commonly affects the lungs (pulmonary TB), but it can also affect other organs such as the kidneys, brain, spine, and lymph nodes. TB spreads through the air when a person with active pulmonary TB coughs, sneezes, speaks, or spits. Without early diagnosis and proper treatment, TB can become severe and may be fatal.
Cause: Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Infection occurs when a person inhales tiny airborne droplets released by someone with active pulmonary TB. Although many infected people develop latent TB infection and do not become ill immediately, some progress to active disease, especially if their immune system becomes weakened
Risk_factors: People are at increased risk of developing active TB if they have one or more of the following ;       > HIV infection                                       > Diabetes mellitus                              >  Undernutrition (malnutrition)   > Smoking                                               > Harmful alcohol use                          > Weak immune system                     > Close contact with a person who has active TB                               > Living in crowded or poorly ventilated environments
Severity:
Emergency Level: High                                 
Reason
Tuberculosis is a serious disease. If it is not diagnosed and treated early, it can damage the lungs and other organs, spread to other people, and may result in death. Drug-resistant TB is even more difficult to treat and requires specialized medical care

Description: Pneumonia is an infectious disease that causes inflammation of the air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs. The air sacs may fill with fluid or pus, making breathing difficult and reducing the amount of oxygen that reaches the body. Pneumonia can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi and ranges from mild to life-threatening, especially in young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment greatly improve recovery and reduce complications.
Cause: Pneumonia is caused by microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, and fungi that infect the lungs. Common bacterial causes include Streptococcus pneumoniae, while respiratory viruses such as influenza virus and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are also frequent causes. Infection spreads mainly through respiratory droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes. The risk of illness increases when the body's immune defenses are weakened.
Risk_factors: People are more likely to develop pneumonia if they have one or more of the following risk factors:                    > Children younger than five years      > Adults aged 65 years and older              > Weak immune system                               > Chronic diseases (such as diabetes or heart disease)                                           > Smoking                                                            > Indoor air pollution                                     > Malnutrition                                                       > Exposure to infected individuals
Severity: Emergency level = High           Reason                         Pneumonia can become life-threatening if it is not treated promptly. Severe pneumonia may cause respiratory failure, bloodstream infection (sepsis), or death, particularly in children, older adults, and individuals with weakened immune systems. Early medical evaluation and appropriate treatment are essential

Description: Diarrheal disease is a preventable and treatable infectious disease characterized by the passage of three or more loose or watery stools within 24 hours. It is usually a symptom of an infection affecting the intestinal tract and can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites. If not treated promptly, especially in young children, it can lead to severe dehydration, malnutrition, and even death. Globally, diarrheal disease remains one of the leading causes of illness and death among children under five years of age.
Cause: Diarrheal disease is commonly caused by infections from bacteria, viruses, or parasites. These microorganisms spread through contaminated food, unsafe drinking water, poor sanitation, and inadequate hygiene. Common bacterial causes include Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter. Viral causes include rotavirus and norovirus, while parasites such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium can also cause infection.
Risk_factors: People are at greater risk of diarrheal disease if they have one or more of the following:         > Drinking unsafe or contaminated water                            > Poor sanitation and hygiene       > Lack of handwashing with soap  > Eating contaminated or improperly prepared food                > Malnutrition                                            > Weakened immune system         > Living in overcrowded environments                                             > Children under five years of age
Severity: Emergency level = High            Reason                        Although many cases are mild, diarrheal disease can rapidly become life-threatening because of severe dehydration and electrolyte loss, especially in infants, young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems. Prompt treatment with oral rehydration solution (ORS), zinc supplementation (for children where appropriate), and medical care for severe cases can prevent complications and death.

Description: Intestinal worm infection, also known as soil-transmitted helminthiasis, is a parasitic disease caused by intestinal worms such as roundworms, whipworms, and hookworms. People become infected by swallowing parasite eggs from contaminated soil, food, or water, or through skin contact with contaminated soil in the case of hookworms. These infections are common in tropical and subtropical regions, including Ethiopia, especially where sanitation and access to clean water are limited. Heavy infections can affect nutrition, growth, learning, and overall health.
Cause: Intestinal worm infections are caused by parasitic worms, mainly:   > Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm) > Trichuris trichiura (whipworm)       > Hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus)                                                   The parasites spread through contact with contaminated soil, poor sanitation, inadequate hygiene, and consumption of contaminated food or water.
Risk_factors: People are more likely to develop intestinal worm infections if they:       > Have poor sanitation                               > Lack access to clean water                      > Do not wash hands properly                    > Walk barefoot on contaminated  soil                                                                     > Eat contaminated food                           > Live in tropical or subtropical regions                                                                 > Are school-age children                          > Live in areas with poor hygiene infrastructure
Severity: Emergency Level: Medium  Reason                                           Most intestinal worm infections are mild, but heavy or repeated infections can cause anemia, malnutrition, abdominal pain, intestinal blockage, poor physical growth, and impaired learning in children. Early diagnosis and treatment help prevent these complications.
